top_cited_works.title: Simplified Reaction Mechanisms for the Oxidation of Hydrocarbon Fuels in Flames
top_cited_works.abstract: Simplified reaction mechanisms for the oxidation of hydrocarbon fuels have been examined using a numerical laminar flame model. The types of mechanisms studied include one and two global reaction steps as well as quasi-global mechanisms. Reaction rate parameters were varied in order to provide the best agreement between computed and experimentally observed flame speeds in selected mixtures of fuel and air. The influences of the various reaction rate parameters on the laminar flame properties have been identified, and a simple procedure to determine the best values for the reaction rate parameters is demonstrated. Fuels studied include n-paraffins from methane to n-decane, some methyl-substituted n-paraffins, acetylene, and representative olefin, alcohol and aromatic hydrocarbons. Results show that the often-employed choice of simultaneous first order fuel and oxidizer dependence for global rate expressions cannot yield the correct dependence of flame speed on equivalence ratio or pressure and cannot correctly predict the rich flammability limit. top_cited_works.title: An updated comprehensive kinetic model of hydrogen combustion
top_cited_works.abstract: Abstract A comprehensively tested H 2 /O 2 chemical kinetic mechanism based on the work of Mueller et al. 1 and recently published kinetic and thermodynamic information is presented. The revised mechanism is validated against a wide range of experimental conditions, including those found in shock tubes, flow reactors, and laminar premixed flame. Excellent agreement of the model predictions with the experimental observations demonstrates that the mechanism is comprehensive and has good predictive capabilities for different experimental systems, including new results published subsequent to the work of Mueller et al. 1 , particularly high‐pressure laminar flame speed and shock tube ignition results. The reaction H + OH + M is found to be primarily significant only to laminar flame speed propagation predictions at high pressure. All experimental hydrogen flame speed observations can be adequately fit using any of the several transport coefficient estimates presently available in the literature for the hydrogen/oxygen system simply by adjusting the rate parameters for this reaction within their present uncertainties. © 2004 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. Int J Chem Kinet 36: 566–575, 2004

Ignition delay time of n-heptane under strained flow field in a counterflow configuration
recent_works.abstract: The overall ignition behaviors of n-heptane/nitrogen opposed by oxygen/ozone streams are experimentally observed, by measuring cool flame ignition (CFI) and hot flame ignition (HFI) delay times in a counterflow configuration. In agreement with the measurements, numerical simulations of the ignition process and the evolution of the maximum temperature show that higher strain rates lead to longer HFI delay times. A sensitivity analysis shows that strain rate plays stronger inhibitive impact on HFI delay than diffusivities of major species. On the contrary, strain rate promotes the transition from cool to hot flame behavior, whereas species diffusivities are insensitive to the transition time interval. Flame structures before and after CFI are analyzed along with species flux to explain the impact of strain rate on ignition behaviors. It is found that decomposition of ozone (O 3 → O 2 + O) accelerates the ignition of a cool flame, while R + O 2 → RO 2 reactions accelerate CFI-to-HFI transition. recent_works.title: Experimental Observation of Ammonia Blending and Cracking on Lean Blow-Out Behaviors in a Model Gas Turbine Combustor
recent_works.venue: Journal of Engineering for Gas Turbines and Power
recent_works.abstract: Abstract Ammonia is gaining attention as a carbon-free fuel for internal combustion engines in the context of global decarbonization efforts. However, its low reactivity poses challenges for stable combustion. This study investigates two strategies to enhance ammonia combustion: blending it with hydrocarbon fuels (methane) and partially cracking it to produce a hydrogen/nitrogen mixture. A model gas turbine combustor with optical access has been developed to investigate lean blow-out (LBO) behaviors. Experimental results show significantly different LBO behaviors between pure methane and ammonia, a factor of seven difference in global equivalence ratio. Ammonia blending with methane renders an increase of effective flame volume, thus suppressing overall reactivity, consequently resulting in the increased global equivalence ratio at LBO. Similar LBO behaviors are observed for ammonia cracking simulated by blending ammonia with hydrogen/nitrogen mixture, exhibiting hindered operability by reducing ammonia cracking fraction. Experimental Observation of Ammonia Blending and Cracking on Lean Blow-Out Behaviors in a Model Gas Turbine Combustor
recent_works.abstract: Abstract With a large focus on decarbonization in recent years, the use of ammonia has been proposed as a possible carbon-free fuel for internal combustion engines. The use of ammonia presents technical challenges, since ammonia exhibits considerably low reactivity compared to hydrocarbon fuels, including slow laminar flame speed, low energy density, and significantly narrow flammability. To cope with low reactivity of ammonia combustion, two approaches have been explored; blending with hydrocarbon fuel and/or integrating with ammonia catalysis cracker that converts ammonia to hydrogen/nitrogen mixture. The objectives of this study are to investigate the impacts of ammonia blending on hydrocarbon fuel and to evaluate the required ammonia cracking fraction on the operability of gas turbine combustors. A model gas turbine combustor with optical access has been developed, where the operability limit, lean blow-out (LBO) behaviors, can be experimentally determined by controlling fuel mass flow rate at various air mass flow rates at 1 atm at a maximum of 10 kW of thermal power.
